lessons.plain: Installing physical hardware means getting a server safely into a rack and keeping it powered, connected and cool. A rack is a tall metal frame that holds servers stacked like drawers in a filing cabinet. Each server needs electricity, ideally from two separate sources so one failure does not stop it. It needs neat, labelled network and power cables so people can work on it later without guessing. It also needs a steady flow of cool air, because hot servers slow down, crash or wear out early. Think of it like moving into a flat. You place the heavy furniture first, plug in safely, label the boxes and leave room for air to move.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server has two power supplies so it keeps running if one fails. If you plug both into the same power strip and that strip's breaker trips, what happens to the server, and why?
lessons.teach:
Installing a server covers four jobs: mounting, power, cabling and cooling. A rack is a standard metal frame, usually 19 inches wide. Its height is measured in rack units (U), and one U is 1.75 inches, so a 2U server fills two slots. Servers slide in on rails. The heaviest gear, such as the battery unit and big storage shelves, goes at the bottom so the rack does not tip over.

Power first. A power distribution unit (PDU) is a strip of outlets inside the rack, fed from a building circuit. An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) is a battery unit that carries equipment through short outages and smooths out voltage dips. Many servers have redundant power supplies (PSUs), meaning two units where either one can run the server alone. They only protect you if they draw from different sources: PSU A to PDU A on circuit A, and PSU B to PDU B on circuit B.

Cooling next. Servers pull cool air in at the front and push hot air out the back. In a hot aisle/cold aisle layout, the fronts of two rows face each other across a cold aisle and the backs face each other across a hot aisle, so no server breathes another's exhaust. Blanking panels are plates that cover empty U slots, so hot air cannot loop round to the front.

For cabling, keep power and data cables apart, route them through trays or cable management arms, label both ends, and leave enough slack for the server to slide out.

Here is a worked example with a 2U server that has two 500 W supplies. First, find 2 free U above the heavier gear and fit the rails. Second, plug PSU 1 into PDU A and PSU 2 into PDU B. Third, check capacity. If side B fails, side A must carry the whole server, so PDU A needs at least 500 W of spare headroom. Fourth, fit blanking panels and label the cables.

The classic mistake is plugging both supplies into one PDU. When that single breaker trips, the redundant server goes dark anyway.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is installing a 4U file server with two 800 W redundant power supplies. Its rack has two PDUs: PDU A is rated for 2000 W and already carries 1100 W of other equipment. The technician works through the job like this. Step 1: find 4 free U above the heavy UPS at the bottom of the rack and fit the rails. Step 2: plug PSU 1 into PDU A (circuit A) and PSU 2 into PDU B (circuit B). Step 3: MISSING. Step 4: fit blanking panels over the empty U slots that remain and label both ends of every cable. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Confirm PDU A could carry the full 800 W alone if side B failed. It has 900 W spare, so it fits.
Confirm PDU A has at least 1600 W spare, because both 800 W supplies would fail over to it together.
Move PSU 2 onto PDU A as well, so both supplies share the same 900 W of spare capacity.
Confirm PDU A has at least 400 W spare, because each supply normally carries only half of the server's load.
questions.why: If side B fails, one supply on PDA A must run the whole server, so PDU A needs at least 800 W of headroom, and 2000 W minus 1100 W leaves 900 W, which is enough.

questions.prompt: A hospital's equipment list says a new storage shelf is 3U tall. How much vertical space will it take up in the rack?
choices: 5.25 inches
1.75 inches
3 inches
19 inches
questions.why: One rack unit (U) is 1.75 inches, so 3U is 3 × 1.75 = 5.25 inches. The 19-inch figure is the usual rack width, not a height.

questions.prompt: A university lab sets up two rows of server racks so that the back of every server in row 1 faces the front of every server in row 2. What problem does this layout cause?
choices: Row 1 servers will pull their intake air out of row 2's cold aisle.
None, because the direction servers face only matters for routing data cables.
Row 2 servers take in row 1's hot exhaust as their cooling air.
Blanking panels stop working, because they only block air in a hot aisle/cold aisle layout.
questions.why: Servers blow hot air out of the back and draw air in at the front, so this layout makes row 2 breathe row 1's exhaust. A hot aisle/cold aisle layout prevents this by having fronts face fronts and backs face backs.

questions.prompt: At a retail company, a server with two redundant power supplies has both supplies plugged into the same PDU, which is fed from building circuit 7. The breaker for circuit 7 trips. What happens to the server?
choices: Only one supply shuts off and the other takes over the full load.
It keeps running at reduced performance until the breaker is reset.
It keeps running on its second power supply, because the supplies are redundant.
It loses power, because both supplies lost the single source they shared.
questions.why: Redundant supplies only protect you when they draw from different PDUs on different circuits. When both share one circuit, a single tripped breaker cuts power to both.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would rack and power a new dual-PSU server so it survives a single power failure and stays cool. Name one tradeoff or limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd mount it on rails in free rack units, keeping the heavy gear like the UPS low so the rack stays stable. I'd plug its two power supplies into two different PDUs fed from separate circuits, ideally each backed by a UPS. That way losing one breaker or one strip leaves the other supply running the server. I'd face the server's front to the cold aisle so it pulls in cool air and exhausts into the hot aisle. I'd cover empty slots with blanking panels so hot air can't loop back. Cables get routed separately for power and data, labelled at both ends, with slack so the server can slide out. The limit is capacity. If one side fails, the other PDU has to carry the full load of every server that shifts onto it. So each PDU needs real headroom, which means I can't load either side close to its rating.
rubricPoints: Mounts on rails with heavy equipment low in the rack.
Connects the two power supplies to separate PDUs on separate circuits.
Explains front-to-back airflow and hot aisle/cold aisle orientation.
Mentions blanking panels covering empty rack slots.
Describes labelled, separated cabling with slack for servicing.
Names a limit, such as PDU headroom during failover.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers physical racking, so reasoning through exam-style rack, power and airflow scenarios builds the judgement this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Servers rarely trust a single hard drive. RAID is a way of grouping several drives so the server treats them as one. Depending on the layout, the group can be faster, can survive a drive dying, or both. You always give up some raw space in return. Shared storage means many servers use the same pool of disks over a network instead of each keeping its own. Capacity planning is working out how much usable space you need now and later. Think of a spare tyre: carrying one costs boot space, but it gets you home when a tyre fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have four 2 TB drives and set them up so every piece of data is stored twice on different drives. Roughly how much space can you actually use, and why?
lessons.teach:
RAID (redundant array of independent disks) combines physical drives into one logical volume. It trades raw capacity for speed, fault tolerance (surviving a drive failure), or both. RAID 0 stripes, meaning it splits data across drives for speed. It has no protection, so one failure loses everything. RAID 1 mirrors: two drives hold identical copies, so half the space is usable. RAID 5 stripes data plus parity. Parity is a calculated value that lets the array rebuild one lost drive, and it costs one drive's worth of space. RAID 6 keeps two parity blocks, survives two failures and costs two drives. RAID 10 mirrors drives in pairs, then stripes across the pairs. It is fast, survives one failure per pair and leaves half the space usable. RAID 5 and 6 write more slowly because parity must be recalculated on every write.

Shared storage lets several servers use the same disks. DAS (direct-attached storage) connects to one server only. NAS (network-attached storage) shares files over an ordinary network using file protocols such as NFS or SMB. A SAN (storage area network) is a dedicated network that offers raw disk blocks called LUNs (logical unit numbers), which each server formats as if they were local. A SAN runs over Fibre Channel, a dedicated storage network technology, or over iSCSI, which carries disk commands across normal Ethernet.

Capacity planning sizes usable space for today plus growth. Here is a worked example. A database needs 4 TB now and grows 1 TB a year, so a three-year plan needs 7 TB. Adding 20 percent headroom brings that to about 8.4 TB. In RAID 6 with 2 TB drives, usable space is (drives minus 2) times 2 TB. Six drives give 8 TB, which is short, so you need seven drives for 10 TB. RAID 10 would need ten drives.

A common mistake is treating RAID as a backup. Deletion, corruption and ransomware are copied faithfully to every disk. A degraded RAID 5 array has no protection while it rebuilds, and large drives take hours to rebuild, so a second failure loses data. That is why RAID 6 or 10 suits large drives and critical workloads.

questions.prompt: A design studio is sizing a new RAID 5 file server. It needs 3 TB today and grows 1.5 TB a year, and the plan covers two years. Step 1: 3 TB + (2 x 1.5 TB) = 6 TB. Step 2: add 20 percent headroom, so 6 TB x 1.2 = 7.2 TB. Step 3: in RAID 5 with 2 TB drives, usable space is (drives minus 1) x 2 TB. Step 4 is missing: how many drives are needed?
choices: 6 drives, because two drives' worth of space must be set aside for parity
8 drives, because half of the raw space is lost to copies
4 drives, because (4 - 1) x 2 TB = 6 TB is close enough to 7.2 TB
5 drives, because (5 - 1) x 2 TB = 8 TB is the first total that reaches 7.2 TB
questions.why: RAID 5 loses one drive to parity, so 4 drives give only 6 TB, which falls short, and 5 drives give 8 TB, the smallest count that covers 7.2 TB; 6 drives is the RAID 6 rule and 8 drives is the RAID 10 rule.

questions.prompt: A clinic is building a two-server cluster. Each server must see shared storage as raw disk blocks that it formats itself, as if the disks were local. The clinic wants to use its existing Ethernet switches and not buy a dedicated storage network. Which option fits?
choices: Direct-attached storage cabled to the first server
A NAS that shares folders over SMB
A SAN that presents LUNs over Fibre Channel
A SAN that presents LUNs over iSCSI
questions.why: A SAN offers raw blocks (LUNs) that each server formats, and iSCSI carries those disk commands over ordinary Ethernet, whereas Fibre Channel needs a dedicated storage network and a NAS shares files, not blocks.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm keeps its client files on a RAID 1 mirror. A staff member accidentally deletes a client folder. What happens, and what is the firm's way to recover it?
choices: The deletion is copied to both drives, so the folder must be restored from a separate backup
The array marks itself degraded and rebuilds the folder from parity
The second drive still holds the folder, so the firm can copy it back from the mirror
The folder is safe as long as only one drive has failed
questions.why: A mirror faithfully copies every change, including a deletion, to both drives, so RAID is not a backup and recovery needs a separate backup copy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is setting up a critical, write-heavy order database on 16 TB drives. It must keep protection during the long rebuild that large drives need, and parity overhead on every write would slow the workload too much. Which RAID level fits best?
choices: RAID 6
RAID 10
RAID 5
RAID 0
questions.why: RAID 10 has no parity to recalculate on writes, so it stays fast, and it survives one failure per mirrored pair, which suits large drives and critical data; RAID 5 and 6 write more slowly, RAID 5 is unprotected while it rebuilds, and RAID 0 has no protection at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a RAID level and a type of storage for a new database server, including the tradeoff you accept and one thing RAID does not protect against.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every RAID level trades usable space against speed and fault tolerance. RAID 0 is fast but one dead drive loses everything, so it is not for a database. RAID 1 and RAID 10 mirror data, so we keep only half the raw space, but writes stay fast and rebuilds are quick. RAID 5 and RAID 6 use parity, which wastes less space. The cost is slower writes, and RAID 5 is exposed during long rebuilds on big drives. For a busy database I'd pick RAID 10, or RAID 6 if space matters more than write speed. I'd size it from current data plus expected growth and headroom, counting usable space rather than raw space. If several servers need the same disks, a SAN over iSCSI or Fibre Channel gives them block storage. If they only need shared files, NAS is enough. RAID is still not a backup: deletions and corruption hit every disk, so we need separate backups.
rubricPoints: States that RAID trades usable capacity for speed and/or fault tolerance.
Correctly contrasts mirroring (RAID 1/10) with parity (RAID 5/6), including the parity write penalty.
Sizes capacity from usable space with growth and headroom, not raw drive totals.
Distinguishes DAS, NAS (file-level) and SAN (block-level LUNs over iSCSI or Fibre Channel).
Notes that RAID is not a backup and that rebuilds leave an array vulnerable.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a RAID level and storage type and doing the capacity arithmetic for a given workload is best practised through exam-style scenarios, and no listed mission or engine builds RAID arrays.

lessons.plain: Servers live in racks, often far away, and still need care: parts fail, and the small built-in programs that run the hardware need updates. Out-of-band management is a separate little computer inside the server with its own network port, so you can reach the machine even when its operating system is frozen or switched off. Think of it as a building caretaker's master key that works even when the tenant is unconscious. Firmware upgrades refresh that low-level hardware software. Hot-swappable parts, such as drives, power supplies and fans, can be pulled and replaced while the server keeps running.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server in a data center two hours away has frozen so badly that you cannot log in to its operating system over the normal network. What would you want built into the server so you could still see its screen and restart it without driving there?
lessons.teach:
Out-of-band (OOB) management means controlling a server through a path that does not depend on its operating system or production network. In-band management, by contrast, uses the running OS, for example SSH or Remote Desktop. The OOB path is a baseboard management controller (BMC), a small independent processor on the motherboard with its own power feed and network port. Vendors brand it differently (Dell iDRAC, HPE iLO), and common standards to talk to it are IPMI (older) and Redfish (a newer web-style interface). A BMC typically offers a remote console (you see the screen and use the keyboard), virtual media (mount an installer image over the network), power on, off and reset, sensor readings, and an event log of hardware faults.

Firmware is the software stored on hardware itself: system BIOS or UEFI, the BMC, RAID controllers, network cards, drives. Upgrades fix bugs and security holes, but a bad one can leave a device unusable. Safe practice: read release notes, check the vendor's compatibility list, back up settings, apply in a maintenance window, follow any required order, and keep stable power during the flash.

Hot-swappable components can be replaced while the server runs; drives in hot-swap bays, redundant power supplies and fans usually qualify, while CPUs and memory usually do not.

Worked example: monitoring reports a server down. Step one, you log in to its BMC on the separate management network. Step two, the remote console shows a hung boot screen. Step three, the hardware event log shows power supply 2 failed. Step four, since supplies are redundant, a technician pulls and replaces PSU 2 without shutting down. Step five, you power-cycle through the BMC and watch it boot.

Common mistake: leaving the BMC on the production network with default credentials. Because the BMC has full control of the machine, an attacker who reaches it effectively owns the server, so it belongs on an isolated management network with strong passwords and current firmware.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a file server in a warehouse 300 km away. Its operating system disk was wiped by mistake, so the server only shows a 'no boot device' message, and nobody is on site. An engineer reinstalls the OS remotely like this. Step 1: she logs in to the server's baseboard management controller (BMC, the small independent management processor on the motherboard) over the separate management network. Step 2: she uses virtual media to mount the OS installer image from her laptop. Step 3: she uses the BMC's power controls to reset the server so it starts from that mounted image. Step 4: ________. Step 5: when the install finishes, she unmounts the image and restarts the server from its local disk. What is Step 4?
choices: Read the BMC hardware event log to follow the installer's progress
Connect to the server over SSH and run the installer from a command prompt
Upgrade the BMC firmware so the mounted installer image will be readable
Open the BMC remote console to see the installer screen and answer its prompts
questions.why: The remote console lets her see the server's screen and use its keyboard without any working OS, while SSH needs a running OS, the event log only records hardware faults, and a firmware upgrade is not needed to use virtual media.

questions.prompt: A technician is updating the firmware on a database server's RAID controller (the card that manages its disk array). Halfway through the flash, the rack loses power for a few seconds. Based on the risks of firmware upgrades, what is the most likely concern?
choices: The RAID controller may be left unusable because its flash was interrupted
Nothing, because firmware only takes effect after the next planned reboot
The BMC will automatically roll the controller back to its previous firmware
The server's operating system will need to be reinstalled before it can boot
questions.why: Firmware is software stored on the device itself, so an interrupted flash can leave that device unusable, which is why stable power during the update is part of safe practice.

questions.prompt: At a retail company, a rack server is running a busy point-of-sale database that cannot be shut down until Sunday night. Monitoring shows four faults on it. Which fault can usually be fixed right now, without powering the server off?
choices: A CPU that is overheating and throttling
A faulty motherboard network port
A failed disk in one of its hot-swap drive bays
A failing memory module in slot B3
questions.why: Drives in hot-swap bays are designed to be replaced while the server runs, whereas memory, CPUs and motherboard parts usually require a shutdown.

questions.prompt: A small design studio plugs the BMC port (iDRAC) of its new server into the same office network as staff laptops and leaves the factory default password in place. Why is this a serious risk?
choices: The BMC will use up network bandwidth and slow down the staff laptops
The server's operating system will refuse to boot while the BMC is on a shared network
Anyone who reaches the BMC can control the whole server, including its power, console and boot media
The BMC's sensor readings become inaccurate when it shares a network with other devices
questions.why: The BMC has full control of the machine independent of the OS, so an attacker who logs in with default credentials effectively owns the server, which is why it belongs on an isolated management network with strong passwords.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we use the server's out-of-band management controller and hot-swap parts for maintenance, and name one risk or limit of each, including firmware upgrades.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every server has a BMC, a small separate computer with its own network port and power, branded iDRAC or iLO and spoken to through IPMI or Redfish. It lets us see the console, mount install media, read hardware logs and power-cycle the box even when the OS is dead, so we avoid a trip to the data center. The tradeoff is that it is a master key: it must live on an isolated management network with strong credentials and patched firmware. Firmware updates fix bugs and vulnerabilities, but a failed flash can brick a device, so we check compatibility, follow the vendor's order, back up settings and use a maintenance window. Hot-swap drives, PSUs and fans can be replaced live, but only if redundancy exists; pulling the wrong drive from a degraded array, or swapping RAM, causes an outage.
rubricPoints: Defines out-of-band management as access independent of the OS and production network via a BMC.
Names what the BMC provides, such as remote console, virtual media, power control and hardware logs.
States the security risk of the BMC and the need for an isolated management network and strong credentials.
Describes safe firmware upgrade practice: compatibility check, backup, ordering, maintenance window.
Identifies typical hot-swappable parts and that CPUs and memory usually are not.
Notes that hot-swap relies on redundancy and the correct component being pulled.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine touches physical hardware, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about choosing OOB tools, sequencing firmware and deciding what can be swapped live builds the judgment this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Installing a server operating system means putting the core software that runs the machine onto its disks so it can boot and do its job. Before the OS goes on, the disk has to be divided and prepared. A partition is a fenced-off section of a disk. A file system is the filing scheme inside that section, deciding how files are named, stored and found. The installation method is how the OS gets there: from a USB stick, over the network, or by copying a ready-made image. Think of a new warehouse. Partitioning builds the rooms, the file system is the shelving system in each room, and the installation method is how the stock is delivered.
lessons.guessPrompt: An old disk layout uses a 32-bit field to count disk sectors. If you install a server with a brand-new 4 TB drive using that old layout, what do you think happens to the space beyond about 2 TB?
lessons.teach:
A partition table is the map at the start of a disk that records where each partition begins and ends. There are two styles. MBR (Master Boot Record) is the older style: it allows four primary partitions, or three plus an extended partition holding logical ones, and it can address only about 2 TB. GPT (GUID Partition Table) is the modern style: it supports disks far larger than 2 TB, many partitions (128 by default on Windows), and keeps a backup copy of the table at the end of the disk. GPT pairs with UEFI, the modern firmware that starts the computer; MBR pairs with legacy BIOS boot.

A file system organizes data inside a partition. Common server choices: NTFS (Windows, with permissions and journaling, meaning it logs changes so it can recover after a crash), ReFS (Windows, built for resilience on large storage), ext4 and XFS (Linux; XFS handles very large files well), VMFS (VMware's shared file system for virtual machine storage) and FAT32 (simple, a 4 GB per-file limit, used for UEFI boot partitions and USB media).

Installation methods include local media (USB or DVD), remote virtual media through an out-of-band management card such as iLO or iDRAC, network boot with PXE (Preboot Execution Environment, where the server pulls its installer from a network server), image deployment (copying a prepared, tested disk image), and unattended installs that read an answer file so nobody has to click through prompts.

Worked example: a database server has a 6 TB RAID volume. Step one, 6 TB exceeds MBR's roughly 2 TB limit, so choose GPT. Step two, GPT boot needs UEFI, so set the firmware to UEFI mode. Step three, the installer creates a small FAT32 EFI system partition and a large XFS data partition. Step four, deploy via PXE with an answer file so ten identical servers build the same way.

Common mistake: leaving firmware in legacy BIOS mode and initializing the disk as MBR. The OS installs, but only about 2 TB is usable, and fixing it later usually means wiping and reinstalling, which costs downtime.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital is installing Windows Server on a new file server with a 4 TB mirrored volume. The server sits in a locked data centre two hours away. Step one: 4 TB is more than MBR's roughly 2 TB limit, so the disk will be initialized as GPT. Step two: ______. Step three: the installer creates a small FAT32 EFI system partition plus a large NTFS partition, so staff file shares get permissions and journaling (a change log used to recover after a crash). Step four: an engineer mounts the installer through the server's out-of-band management card (a separate remote-control board such as iDRAC), so nobody has to travel. Which choice correctly fills step two?
choices: Leave the firmware in legacy BIOS mode, because Windows Server will still boot from the GPT disk
Set the firmware to UEFI mode, because booting from a GPT disk requires UEFI
Format the EFI system partition as NTFS, so it shares permissions with the data partition
Initialize the disk as MBR with an extended partition, so more than four partitions are available
questions.why: GPT is paired with UEFI firmware, so the firmware has to be switched to UEFI mode before the OS installs onto the GPT disk.

questions.prompt: A partition table is the map at the start of a disk that records where each partition begins and ends. Which feature does a GPT (GUID Partition Table) disk have that an MBR (Master Boot Record) disk lacks?
choices: Support for exactly four primary partitions
Compatibility only with legacy BIOS boot
A backup copy of the partition table stored at the end of the disk
A built-in 4 GB per-file size limit
questions.why: GPT keeps a second copy of its table at the end of the disk; the four-partition limit and the BIOS pairing belong to MBR, and the 4 GB per-file limit belongs to FAT32.

questions.prompt: A shipping company must reinstall the OS on a server at a small port office that has no IT staff on site. The server has an out-of-band management card, a separate board such as iLO that allows remote control of the server even when no OS is running. Which installation method fits best?
choices: Insert a USB stick into the server's front port
Copy files to the existing OS before wiping it
Run the installer from a DVD in the server's drive
Attach the installer as remote virtual media through the card
questions.why: Remote virtual media through an out-of-band card lets an administrator present the installer to the server over the network, with no one physically present.

questions.prompt: A technician formats a USB drive as FAT32 to carry a prepared 7 GB server disk image to a lab, but the copy fails even though the drive has 32 GB free. What is the most likely cause?
choices: FAT32 cannot store a single file larger than 4 GB
The image must be deployed with PXE instead
FAT32 only works on UEFI boot partitions
The drive was not initialized as GPT
questions.why: FAT32 has a 4 GB per-file limit, so a 7 GB file cannot be written no matter how much free space the drive has.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a partition style, a file system and an installation method for a new server, and name one limit or tradeoff that affects the choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I check disk size and firmware. If the disk is over 2 TB, or the server uses UEFI, I pick GPT, because MBR tops out around 2 TB and only allows four primary partitions. GPT also keeps a backup copy of the partition table. Next I pick the file system for the OS and workload: NTFS or ReFS on Windows, ext4 or XFS on Linux, VMFS if it is VMware datastore storage, and FAT32 only for the small UEFI boot partition because it caps files at 4 GB. For installation, one server can be done from USB or remote virtual media through the management card, but for many identical servers I would use PXE or an image with an answer file so builds are consistent. The tradeoff is that automated methods need setup work up front, and a wrong partition choice usually means reinstalling.
rubricPoints: MBR is limited to about 2 TB and four primary partitions, while GPT supports larger disks and many partitions.
GPT boots with UEFI firmware and MBR with legacy BIOS.
The file system is matched to the OS and workload, such as NTFS/ReFS, ext4/XFS, VMFS or FAT32.
Installation methods include local or virtual media, PXE network boot, imaging and unattended answer files.
Automated methods give consistent builds at scale but need upfront setup.
A wrong partition style choice often forces a wipe and reinstall.

suggested.rationale: No current mission builds a server from bare disks, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that pair disk size, firmware and fleet size with the right partition, file system and install method builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Every server needs a place on the network and a name people can find. An IP address is its numeric street address. DNS is the phone book that turns a friendly name like files01 into that number. DHCP is a receptionist that hands out addresses to devices automatically so nobody types them by hand. A VLAN is a way of splitting one physical switch into several separate, private networks, like putting walls inside one open-plan office. Configuring network services means giving a server a stable address, a correct name, and a seat in the right network segment.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a server's network address changed every few days on its own, what do you think would happen to users who reach it by its name?
lessons.teach:
An IP address is the number a device uses on a network, such as 10.0.20.15. A subnet mask (for example 255.255.255.0, written /24) marks which part names the network and which part names the host. Devices in the same subnet talk directly. The default gateway is the router a server sends traffic to when the destination is outside its subnet. DNS (Domain Name System) translates names into addresses. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, an AAAA record maps one to an IPv6 address, and a PTR record does the reverse, from address to name. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) hands out addresses automatically from a scope, which is the pool of addresses for one subnet. Along with the address it gives the mask, the gateway and the DNS server. A reservation tells DHCP to always give one device the same address. It recognizes that device by its MAC address, the hardware ID of its network card. A VLAN (virtual LAN) splits one physical switch into separate logical networks, each usually its own subnet. An access port carries one VLAN, untagged. A trunk port carries many VLANs by tagging each frame with its VLAN ID.

Servers get a static address (set by hand) or a reservation, because clients find them by name and DNS must point at an address that stays put.

Worked example: a file server joins VLAN 20, subnet 10.0.20.0/24, gateway 10.0.20.1. Step 1: set its switch port as an access port on VLAN 20. Step 2: assign 10.0.20.15/24 statically, with gateway 10.0.20.1 and DNS server 10.0.20.5. Exclude .15 from the DHCP scope. Step 3: create an A record files01 pointing to 10.0.20.15, plus a matching PTR record. Step 4: from a client, look up files01 and confirm it returns 10.0.20.15.

Common mistake: leaving a server on an ordinary DHCP lease. If its address changes, the A record still points at the old address. Users then see 'server not found' even though the server is healthy. A related mistake is setting a static address inside the DHCP scope. DHCP may later hand that same address to a laptop, and the two devices conflict.

questions.prompt: A clinic is bringing a new database server, db02, into production on VLAN 40, subnet 172.16.40.0/24, gateway 172.16.40.1, DNS server 172.16.40.4. The admin wants the server to keep a fixed address but still get its settings from DHCP. Step 1: set the server's switch port as an access port on VLAN 40. Step 2: note the MAC address of the server's network card and create a DHCP reservation in the 172.16.40.0/24 scope so that this card always receives 172.16.40.25. Step 3: ______ (the step that lets clients reach the server by typing the name db02). Step 4: from a client, look up db02 and confirm it returns 172.16.40.25. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Set the server's default gateway to 172.16.40.25
Create an AAAA record named db02 that points to 172.16.40.25
Create an A record named db02 that points to 172.16.40.25
Create a PTR record that maps 172.16.40.25 to db02
questions.why: Clients find the server by name, and an A record is the DNS entry that turns the name db02 into the IPv4 address 172.16.40.25. A PTR record only goes from address to name, and an AAAA record is for IPv6 addresses.

questions.prompt: A web server is set to 10.8.4.20 with mask 255.255.255.0 (/24). It needs to send traffic to a backup server at 10.8.9.50. Where does the web server send that traffic first?
choices: To its DNS server, which forwards the traffic to 10.8.9.50
To its default gateway, because 10.8.9.50 is outside its subnet
Directly to 10.8.9.50, because both addresses start with 10.8
To the DHCP server, which assigns a route to 10.8.9.50
questions.why: With a /24 mask, 10.8.4.x and 10.8.9.x are different subnets, so the server hands the traffic to its default gateway, the router for destinations outside its own subnet.

questions.prompt: At a law firm, the DHCP scope for subnet 192.168.50.0/24 hands out addresses .50 through .200. An admin sets a new print server statically to 192.168.50.60 and changes nothing in DHCP. What problem is most likely later on?
choices: DHCP may give 192.168.50.60 to another device, causing an address conflict
The print server's A record will stop working when its DHCP lease ends
The switch will drop the print server's frames because they are untagged
The print server will lose its default gateway after a reboot
questions.why: The static address sits inside the scope, so DHCP still treats it as free and may hand it to another device, leaving two devices on one address; it should have been excluded from the scope.

questions.prompt: A single switch port connects to a virtualization host that runs virtual machines on VLANs 10, 20 and 30. How should that switch port be configured?
choices: As a trunk port, so each frame is tagged with its VLAN ID
As an access port with a DHCP reservation for each VLAN
As three separate subnets on one access port, without any tagging
As an access port on VLAN 10, so all three VLANs share it untagged
questions.why: An access port carries only one VLAN untagged, while a trunk port carries many VLANs by tagging each frame with its VLAN ID, which is what a host serving three VLANs needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a new server its network identity, covering its address, its name, and its VLAN. Name one tradeoff between a static address and a DHCP reservation.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd find out which VLAN the server belongs in, because each VLAN is usually its own subnet. The switch port has to be an access port on that VLAN, or a trunk if the server carries several. Next, the server needs an address that doesn't change, because clients reach it by name. That means either a static address outside the DHCP scope or a DHCP reservation tied to its MAC address. It also needs the right mask, gateway and DNS server. Then I'd add an A record and a PTR record and test the lookup from a client. The tradeoff: a static address doesn't depend on the DHCP server being up, but it's managed by hand and can collide if it sits inside the scope. A reservation keeps addressing central, but it depends on DHCP being available, and it breaks if the network card is replaced and the MAC changes.
rubricPoints: Servers need a stable address via static assignment or a DHCP reservation.
DNS A and PTR records must match the server's address and be tested.
Mask, gateway and DNS server settings are part of the configuration.
The server's VLAN and switch port type (access or trunk) must match its subnet.
Static addresses must be kept out of the DHCP scope to avoid conflicts.
A tradeoff between static and reserved addressing is named.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet across subnets, gateways and VLAN segments in a virtual network path tracer makes the learner apply addressing and segmentation rather than just recall the terms.

lessons.plain: Managing server functions means deciding what jobs a server does, watching how well it does them, and moving its data safely when things change. A role is a job the server is set up for, such as file sharing, web hosting or name lookup. Monitoring is keeping an eye on numbers called performance metrics, like how busy the processor is or how full the disk is. Data migration is moving data from one place to another without losing or corrupting it. Think of a restaurant kitchen: each station has a role, the manager watches ticket times, and a move to a new kitchen is planned for a quiet night.
lessons.guessPrompt: A file server's processor normally sits around 20% busy. Today it shows 85% all afternoon. Before reading anything, what would you want to know before deciding whether this is a problem?
lessons.teach:
A server role is a defined job installed on a server, such as file server, web server, database server, or directory service (the central list of users and computers). Installing only the roles a workload needs keeps the system simpler, uses fewer resources, and leaves fewer services an attacker could target.

Monitoring means collecting performance metrics over time. A metric is a measured number. The core ones are CPU utilization (the percentage of time the processor is busy), memory usage (how much RAM is in use, plus paging, which is swapping memory to disk when RAM runs short), disk I/O (input/output, often counted as IOPS, input/output operations per second), disk latency (how long each read or write waits), and network throughput (data moved per second). A baseline is a record of normal values, captured when the server is healthy. A threshold is the value that triggers an alert, an automatic notification.

Worked example: a baseline shows CPU at 20% and disk latency at 5 ms. Today CPU reads 85%. Step one, compare it to the baseline: the reading is far above normal. Step two, check related metrics: memory is near full and paging is high. Step three, conclude that the system is short of RAM. It is swapping memory to disk, and that extra work is driving the CPU up. The fix is more RAM or a lighter workload, not a faster CPU.

Data migration moves data to new storage or a new server. A sound plan backs up the data first, copies it, and verifies it with checksums (fingerprints of the data) or by comparing file counts. It then schedules a cutover, the moment users switch over, inside a maintenance window and keeps a rollback path.

A common mistake is judging a metric without a baseline, or reacting to one number alone. The result in a running system is wasted money on the wrong upgrade while the real bottleneck, the resource limiting performance, keeps slowing users down.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's file server feels slow to staff. Its baseline, recorded when it was healthy, shows CPU at 15%, memory at 50% with almost no paging, disk latency at 3 ms and network throughput at 200 Mbps. Today's readings: CPU 18%, memory 55% with almost no paging, disk latency 45 ms, network throughput 190 Mbps, and disk IOPS (input/output operations per second) about double the baseline. Step one: compare to the baseline. Disk latency, the time each read or write waits, is fifteen times normal. Step two: ______. Step three: conclude that the disk is the bottleneck, the resource limiting performance. The fix is faster storage or less disk load, not more RAM or a faster CPU. Which choice correctly fills in step two?
choices: Raise the disk latency alert threshold to 50 ms so the notification stops firing and staff are no longer disturbed.
Upgrade the CPU first, because the processor is the most important metric on any server, then recheck the disk later.
Check related metrics. CPU and network sit near baseline, and memory is normal with almost no paging, so swapping is not causing the disk load.
Skip the baseline and judge the 45 ms reading against a general rule of thumb, since past values on this server do not matter.
questions.why: Checking related metrics rules out other causes, such as RAM shortage driving paging to disk, before you name the disk as the real bottleneck.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a logistics company is about to set up monitoring on a newly built warehouse server. Before setting any alert thresholds, she records CPU, memory, disk latency and network throughput over a week of normal, healthy operation. What has she created?
choices: A checksum, a fingerprint used to confirm data was copied correctly
A cutover, the moment users switch to the new server
A baseline, a record of normal values to compare future readings against
A threshold, the value that triggers an automatic notification
questions.why: A baseline is a record of a server's normal metric values, captured while it is healthy, so that later readings can be judged as normal or abnormal.

questions.prompt: A city library is migrating its catalogue database from an old server to new storage. The team has already backed up the data and copied it to the new storage. What should they do next, before scheduling the cutover?
choices: Raise the alert thresholds on the new server so migration activity does not cause alerts
Verify the copy by comparing checksums or file counts between the old and new locations
Delete the data on the old server at once to free space, since the copy has finished
Switch users over immediately during business hours to test the copy under real load
questions.why: A sound migration plan verifies the copied data with checksums or file counts before the cutover, and keeps the original as part of the rollback path.

questions.prompt: An administrator is building a server whose only job is to act as a print server for a small office. He also installs the web server, database server and directory service roles 'just in case they're needed later.' What is the most likely result?
choices: The server becomes more secure, because more roles give it more layers of protection
The server uses more resources, becomes more complex and has more services an attacker could target
Print performance improves, because the unused roles share their resources with printing
The server's baseline becomes unnecessary, because extra roles report their own metrics
questions.why: Installing only the roles a workload needs keeps the system simpler and lighter, and it leaves fewer services exposed to attack. Unneeded roles reverse all three of those benefits.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a server needs a performance baseline before you set monitoring alerts. Walk through how you would use it to find a bottleneck, and name one limit or tradeoff of alert thresholds.
lessons.modelAnswer: A baseline is a record of what normal looks like for this particular server: typical CPU, memory, paging, disk latency, IOPS and network throughput, captured while it is healthy. Without one, a number like 70% CPU means nothing, because for one server it is normal and for another it is a crisis. With a baseline, I compare current readings against normal and then look at related metrics together. If CPU is high and paging is also high, memory is probably the real bottleneck, and buying a faster CPU would not help. I set alert thresholds a sensible margin above the baseline. The tradeoff is that a threshold set too low floods people with false alarms until they start ignoring them, while one set too high misses real trouble. Baselines also go stale when roles or workloads change, so I re-capture them after changes such as a data migration.
rubricPoints: Defines a baseline as the recorded normal values for that specific server.
Names core metrics such as CPU, memory and paging, disk IOPS or latency, and network throughput.
Explains comparing current readings to the baseline and correlating several metrics to find the true bottleneck.
Notes the threshold tradeoff between false alarms and missed problems.
Mentions that baselines must be refreshed after role or workload changes.

suggested.rationale: Finding what is burning the CPU and stopping it properly makes the learner read live performance metrics and trace an abnormal reading back to its cause, which is the core monitoring skill here.

lessons.plain: High availability means arranging servers so a service keeps running even when one machine fails. The idea is to remove any single point of failure, a part whose loss takes everything down. Clustering groups several servers so they act as one service and watch each other. Load balancing spreads incoming requests across several servers so none is overwhelmed. Failover is the handover: when one server dies, another takes over its work. Think of a restaurant with several cooks. Orders are shared among them, and if one goes home sick, the others pick up the tickets so diners barely notice.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two servers run the same website and both are always serving traffic. One crashes during a busy hour. What do you think happens to the visitors, and what new problem might the surviving server face?
lessons.teach:
High availability (HA) is designing a service to stay up despite component failures. It works by adding redundancy (spare capacity that can carry the load) so there is no single point of failure.

A cluster is a group of servers, called nodes, that present one service. Nodes send each other a heartbeat, a small "I'm alive" signal sent every few seconds. In an active-passive cluster, one node serves while a standby waits. In an active-active cluster, every node serves at once. Failover is moving the workload to a healthy node when the heartbeat stops. Failback is returning it to the original node once it is repaired. Quorum is a voting rule: a group of nodes may run the service only if it holds a majority of votes. This prevents split-brain, where two halves of a cluster lose contact and both try to own the same data, which can corrupt it. A small extra voter, called a witness, breaks ties in two-node clusters.

A load balancer is a device or service that sits in front of the nodes and distributes requests. Round robin sends requests to each node in turn. Least connections sends each request to the node currently handling the fewest. Health checks are regular test requests; a node that fails them is removed from the rotation.

Worked example: a two-node active-passive database cluster with a witness. Node A serves. Node A's power supply dies, so its heartbeat stops. Node B and the witness together hold two of three votes, a majority, so B claims quorum. B takes over the shared storage and the service address. Clients reconnect after a short pause. Later A is repaired, and an administrator schedules failback during a quiet hour.

A common mistake is sizing an active-active pair at 70% load each. When one node fails, the survivor must carry 140% of its capacity and slows or crashes. That turns one failure into a full outage, so each node must be able to carry the whole load alone.

questions.prompt:
A veterinary clinic runs a three-node file-service cluster. The nodes are Alpha, Bravo and Charlie, and each holds one vote. Alpha is currently serving clients. A network switch fails, cutting Alpha off from Bravo and Charlie, though all three machines stay powered on.

Step 1: Alpha stops receiving heartbeats from Bravo and Charlie, and they stop receiving Alpha's heartbeat.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: Bravo takes over the shared storage and the service address, and clients reconnect after a short pause.
Step 4: The switch is replaced, and an administrator schedules failback to Alpha during a quiet hour.

Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Bravo and Charlie hold two of three votes, a majority, so they claim quorum. Alpha holds only one vote, so it stops running the service.
Alpha claims quorum because it was running the service, so Bravo and Charlie wait until the switch is fixed.
Alpha keeps serving because it was the active node, and Bravo also starts serving, so clients can reach both sides.
Neither side may run the service, because quorum always requires a witness, and this cluster has none.
questions.why: Quorum lets only the side holding a majority of votes run the service, which prevents split-brain; here that is Bravo and Charlie, with two of three votes.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore puts a load balancer in front of three web servers and sets it to use least connections. At the moment a new request arrives, Server 1 is handling 42 connections, Server 2 is handling 17, and Server 3 is handling 29. All three servers are passing their health checks. Which server receives the new request?
choices: Server 1, because it is first in the list.
Server 2, because it is handling the fewest connections.
Whichever server received the previous request, to keep sessions together.
Server 3, because it is the next server in turn.
questions.why: Least connections sends each new request to the node currently handling the fewest connections, and that is Server 2 with 17.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs an active-active pair of application servers. During normal peak hours, each node runs at 65% of its own capacity. One node's motherboard fails at peak. What is the most likely result?
choices: The survivor carries 65% of its capacity, because each node's load stays the same after failover.
Nothing changes for users, because active-active clusters do not need to fail over.
The survivor runs at about 100%, because the load balancer drops the excess requests safely.
The survivor must carry about 130% of its capacity, so it slows or crashes, and one failure can become a full outage.
questions.why: In an active-active pair, the survivor inherits both nodes' load (65% + 65% = 130%), which is more than it can handle, so each node should be sized to carry the whole load alone.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm builds a two-node cluster with no witness. Each node holds one vote. The network link between the two nodes breaks, but both nodes stay running. Why is this design a problem?
choices: Both nodes will lose their heartbeat signal permanently and must be rebuilt from scratch.
The load balancer will switch from round robin to least connections and overload one node.
Each node will immediately fail back to the other, so the service will keep bouncing between them.
With one vote each, neither side holds a majority to decide ownership; a witness is the tie-breaker that avoids split-brain and data corruption.
questions.why: In a two-node cluster, a lost link leaves a 1-to-1 tie with no majority, and a witness supplies the extra vote so that only one side owns the data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between active-active and active-passive clustering, how failover actually happens, and one tradeoff or limit they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both designs use a cluster of nodes that exchange heartbeats so each knows the others are alive. In active-passive, one node does the work and a standby waits. If the heartbeat stops, the standby takes over the service address and storage. That is failover. Active-active runs every node at once, usually behind a load balancer that uses health checks to stop sending traffic to a dead node. The tradeoff is cost against capacity. Passive hardware sits idle, but it is guaranteed to have room for the full load. Active-active uses everything, but only if each node is sized to carry the whole load alone, otherwise one failure overloads the survivor. Either way, we need quorum, usually with a witness in a two-node setup, so a network split cannot cause split-brain, where both sides write to the same data.
rubricPoints: Defines active-passive as one serving node with a waiting standby, and active-active as all nodes serving.
Explains that missed heartbeats or failed health checks trigger failover to a healthy node.
Mentions the load balancer's role in distributing requests and removing unhealthy nodes.
Names quorum or a witness as protection against split-brain.
States a tradeoff, such as idle standby cost or needing each node sized to carry the full load.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios like choosing a cluster type or predicting what happens after a node fails, and no current mission or planned engine directly builds clusters, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Virtualization lets one physical server pretend to be several separate computers at once. The real machine is the host. Each pretend computer is a guest, also called a virtual machine, and it runs its own operating system as if it owned the hardware. A layer of software called a hypervisor hands out slices of the host's processor, memory and disk to each guest. Think of an apartment building: one structure, shared plumbing and power, but each tenant has a locked, private flat. Cloud models extend the idea: they describe who owns the building and how much of the work you do yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server has 128 GB of memory and you want to run eight virtual machines on it, each given 16 GB. Do you think that will work smoothly under load? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Virtualization runs several isolated computers on one physical machine. The host is the physical server. A guest, or virtual machine (VM), is a software-defined computer with its own operating system. The hypervisor is the layer that shares the host's hardware among guests. A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor installs directly on the hardware and is the normal choice for production servers. A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on an ordinary operating system and suits labs and desktops.

Resource allocation is how you divide the host. A vCPU is a virtual processor that a guest sees, and the hypervisor schedules it onto real cores. Overcommitment means promising guests more vCPUs or memory than physically exist, betting that they will not all peak at once. Thin provisioning creates a virtual disk that grows as data is written. Thick provisioning reserves the disk's full size up front.

Worked example: a host has 16 cores and 128 GB of RAM. You plan eight guests, each with 4 vCPUs and 16 GB. CPU: 8 × 4 = 32 vCPUs, a 2:1 ratio, which is usually fine because idle vCPUs cost little. Memory: 8 × 16 = 128 GB, which leaves nothing for the hypervisor itself, so guests would swap to disk under load. Trim each guest to 14 GB (112 GB in total) or move one guest to another host.

Common mistake: overcommitting memory as freely as CPU. Contention for CPU only makes guests slower. Running out of memory forces paging and can crash guests. Thin disks carry a similar risk, because if the shared storage fills up, every guest on it can stop writing at once.

Cloud models describe who owns and runs the infrastructure. The deployment models are public cloud (provider hardware shared and rented on demand), private cloud (dedicated to one organization), hybrid cloud (public and private connected together) and community cloud (shared by organizations with common needs). The service models are IaaS, where you get virtual machines and networks to manage yourself; PaaS, a managed platform where you deploy only your code; and SaaS, a finished application. Going from IaaS to SaaS, you manage less but also control less.

questions.prompt: A small clinic is sizing one host with 24 physical cores and 256 GB of RAM. It plans twelve guests (virtual machines), each with 4 vCPUs and 24 GB of memory. Step 1, CPU: 12 × 4 = 48 vCPUs on 24 cores, a 2:1 ratio, which is acceptable because idle vCPUs cost little. Step 2, memory: [missing]. Step 3, fix: shrink each guest to 20 GB (240 GB in total), leaving 16 GB for the hypervisor itself. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: 12 × 24 = 288 GB, more than the 256 GB installed, so memory is overcommitted and guests would page to disk or crash under load.
12 × 24 = 288 GB, which is over the limit, but memory contention only makes the guests run a little slower, like CPU contention.
12 × 24 = 288 GB, but memory can be overcommitted at 2:1 just like CPU, so the plan is fine as written.
12 × 4 = 48 GB of memory in use, far below the 256 GB installed, so memory is not a concern.
questions.why: Twelve guests at 24 GB each need 288 GB, which is more than the host physically has, and running short of memory causes paging and possible crashes, not just slowdown.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to run two test virtual machines on her everyday laptop, which already runs a normal desktop operating system she must keep using. Which kind of hypervisor fits this situation?
choices: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor, installed directly on the laptop's hardware in place of her operating system
Thick provisioning, because it reserves the full disk size for each test machine
A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor, installed as an application on the existing operating system
A hybrid cloud, because it connects her laptop to a public provider
questions.why: A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on an ordinary operating system, which suits desktops and labs where that operating system must stay in place.

questions.prompt: A web hosting company gives 30 guests thin-provisioned 200 GB virtual disks, all stored on one shared 2 TB storage pool, and the guests keep adding data. What is the main risk of this setup?
choices: Each guest immediately reserves its full 200 GB, so the pool is full on the first day
The guests will run slower because their vCPUs are scheduled onto fewer real cores
Thin disks cannot grow, so each guest will be stuck at whatever size it started with
If the shared pool fills up, every guest on it can stop being able to write at the same moment
questions.why: Thin disks grow as data is written, so together they can outgrow the shared storage, and when it fills, all the guests on it lose the ability to write at once.

questions.prompt: A retail company wants to put its own web application code online but does not want to install, patch or manage the operating systems or servers underneath. Which cloud service model matches this need?
choices: SaaS, because the company would write and deploy its own application
Private cloud, because the hardware is dedicated to one organization
PaaS, because the provider runs the platform and the company deploys only its code
IaaS, because the company gets virtual machines and networks to manage itself
questions.why: PaaS is a managed platform where you deploy only your code, so the provider handles the operating systems and servers underneath it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a host and a guest, how you would decide how much CPU and memory to give guests on one host, and one risk or tradeoff of overcommitting resources.
lessons.modelAnswer: The host is the physical server. A guest is a virtual machine running its own operating system on top of it. The hypervisor sits between them and shares out the hardware. Production uses Type 1, which runs straight on the hardware, while Type 2 runs inside a normal operating system and is fine for labs. When I size guests, I add up the vCPUs and memory I am promising and compare the totals with real cores and RAM, leaving headroom for the hypervisor. CPU can safely be overcommitted a bit, say 2:1, because idle vCPUs cost little and contention only slows guests down. Memory is riskier: if the guests together actually use more than exists, the host pages to disk and guests can crash. Thin-provisioned disks have the same trap, because full storage stops every guest at once. The tradeoff is better use of the hardware against the risk of everyone peaking together.
rubricPoints: Defines the host as the physical machine and a guest as a VM with its own OS.
Describes the hypervisor and the difference between Type 1 and Type 2.
Sizes guests by comparing total allocated vCPUs and memory with physical capacity, leaving hypervisor headroom.
Explains that overcommitment trades efficiency for the risk of contention when guests peak together.
Notes that memory or thin-disk exhaustion is more dangerous than CPU contention.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine builds VMs, so reasoning through exam-style sizing and cloud-model scenarios best tests this objective.

lessons.plain: A script is a plain text file holding a list of commands that the computer runs in order, so a job you would otherwise type by hand happens the same way every time. Think of it as a recipe card: a variable is a labelled bowl that holds an ingredient, a loop says 'repeat this step for every egg', and a condition says 'only if the oven is hot'. Server administrators write scripts to check services, create user accounts, clean up old logs and prepare new servers, so routine work is fast, repeatable and less error-prone.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to create the same 40 user accounts on five new servers. Typing each one by hand takes about a minute. Roughly how long would that take, and what kinds of mistakes might creep in that a script would avoid?
lessons.teach:
A script is a text file of commands run by an interpreter, which is a program that reads the commands and carries them out one at a time. Common types are Bash (.sh) on Linux, PowerShell (.ps1) and batch (.bat) on Windows, and older VBScript (.vbs).

A variable is a named slot that holds a value so you can reuse or change it. Values have basic data types: a string is text, an integer is a whole number, a boolean is true or false, and an array is an ordered list. An environment variable is one the operating system provides to every program, such as the current user's name or the search path for commands. A conditional (if/else) runs code only when a test passes. The test uses comparators such as equal, not equal, greater than and less than. A loop repeats code: a for loop runs once per item in a list, and a while loop keeps going as long as a condition stays true.

Worked example: a service-check script. Step 1: store the array services = web, dns, backup. Step 2: a for loop takes the first item, so the variable svc holds 'web'. Step 3: the script asks the OS for web's status, which comes back 'running'. The conditional status not equal to 'running' is false, so nothing happens. Step 4: svc becomes 'dns', its status is 'stopped', the test is true, so the script restarts dns and writes a line to a log. Step 5: it checks 'backup' the same way, and the loop ends because the list is used up.

Other common server tasks are startup and shutdown routines, login scripts, creating accounts in bulk, deleting old log files, and bootstrapping a new server.

A common mistake is a while loop whose condition never changes, for example waiting for a service that never starts. This creates an infinite loop. On a running server it can burn CPU or block the next job, so add a counter or timeout and test scripts on a non-production machine first.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic runs a nightly cleanup script on its file server. Step 1: store the array logs = app.log (45 days old), audit.log (10 days old), mail.log (60 days old). Step 2: a for loop takes the first item, so the variable file holds 'app.log'. The conditional 'age greater than 30 days' is true, so the script deletes app.log. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: file becomes 'mail.log'. Its age of 60 is greater than 30, the test is true, so mail.log is deleted. Step 5: the list is used up, so the loop ends. What happens in Step 3?
choices: The variable file becomes 'audit.log'. Its age of 10 is not greater than 30, so the test is false, audit.log is kept, and the loop moves on.
The variable file becomes 'audit.log'. The script keeps rechecking it until it reaches 30 days old, then deletes it.
The variable file becomes 'audit.log'. Its age of 10 is less than 30, so the test is true and audit.log is deleted.
The variable file becomes 'audit.log'. Its age of 10 is not greater than 30, so the test is false and the loop ends there.
questions.why: A for loop runs once per item in the list, so a false test only skips that one file and the loop continues to the next item.

questions.prompt: An administrator at a logistics firm is writing a script to create accounts in bulk. The script must hold the 40 new usernames as one ordered list that a loop can step through. Which data type fits this variable best?
choices: String
Boolean
Integer
Array
questions.why: An array is an ordered list of values, so it can hold all 40 usernames for a loop to work through one at a time.

questions.prompt: A login script at a school district needs the name of whoever is signing in, so it can map that person's home folder. The admin does not want to type any names into the script. Where should the script get the name from?
choices: An environment variable the operating system provides to every program
A boolean the script sets to true when someone logs in
A conditional that compares the name to 'not equal'
A for loop over every user account in the district
questions.why: Environment variables are supplied by the operating system to every program and include values such as the current user's name, so nothing has to be hard-coded.

questions.prompt: A startup script on a production server contains a while loop. The loop keeps running for as long as a network file share reports 'offline'. One morning the share's hardware has failed, so it stays offline. What is the most likely result, and what is the best way to prevent it?
choices: The interpreter turns the while loop into a for loop and moves on. Rename the file to .bat to fix it.
The loop ends at once because the share is offline. Replace the condition with a string to stop this.
The loop never ends, which can burn CPU or block the next job. Add a counter or timeout, and test the script on a non-production machine first.
The loop stops by itself after one pass because the condition is true. No change is needed.
questions.why: A while loop repeats while its condition stays true, so a condition that never changes creates an infinite loop. A counter or timeout gives the loop a guaranteed way to end.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how variables, loops and conditionals work together in a script that checks and restarts services, and name one risk or tradeoff of automating that task.
lessons.modelAnswer: A script is a text file of commands that an interpreter, such as Bash or PowerShell, runs in order. Variables hold values we reuse. For example, an array can list the services to check, and another variable holds the one we are on right now. A for loop walks through that list one item at a time. Inside the loop, a conditional compares the service's status to 'running' and restarts it only if the two do not match, then logs what it did. That turns a manual check across many services into one repeatable action. The tradeoff is that a script repeats its mistakes as faithfully as its successes. A bad comparison could restart healthy services, and a while loop with no exit can hang or eat CPU. So add timeouts, log every action, and test on a non-production server before scheduling it.
rubricPoints: Defines a script as commands run in order by an interpreter such as Bash or PowerShell.
Explains that variables hold values, including lists or arrays of items.
Explains that a loop repeats work for each item or while a condition holds.
Explains that a conditional with a comparator decides whether an action runs.
Names a real risk, such as infinite loops or mass mistakes, and a safeguard like testing, timeouts or logging.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner write loops, conditions and variables against real log data, which is the core scripting skill this objective describes.

lessons.plain: Asset management means knowing exactly what equipment you own, where it is, what state it is in, and what paperwork goes with it, from the day it is bought until the day it is safely thrown away. Think of it like keeping a careful file for every car in a company fleet: the plate number, purchase receipt, service history, warranty, and the date it goes to the scrapyard. For servers, the same file also holds diagrams and recovery instructions. Those must be kept up to date and stored somewhere safe but reachable, even when the server itself is down.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's disk fails at 2 a.m. and the recovery instructions are saved only as a file on that same server. What problem do you expect, and where would you rather have kept them?
lessons.teach:
Asset management is tracking every piece of hardware and software through its whole life. Each server gets an asset tag, a company-issued label with a unique number, recorded in an inventory with its make, model, serial number (the maker's unique ID), location, owner, proof of purchase, and whether it is owned or leased (rented, so it must go back on a set date). The record also holds warranty and support-contract dates, so you know who pays for repairs.

Lifecycle management follows four stages: procurement (choosing and buying), usage (installed, patched, monitored), end of life or EOL (the vendor stops selling or supporting it, so no more fixes), and disposal or recycling, where drives are securely wiped or physically destroyed and the asset is removed from inventory.

Documentation is the written knowledge around assets: service manuals, infrastructure and architecture diagrams (what connects to what), workflow diagrams, baselines (records of normal performance and configuration), server configurations, recovery procedures, and change-management records (an approved log of every change). It also captures agreed targets such as an SLA, a service level agreement promising uptime. Why it works: when something breaks, nobody has to guess.

Worked example: a drive light turns amber. You read the asset tag, look it up, and find the serial number and that the warranty runs another eight months. You open a replacement request with the vendor, follow the documented recovery procedure, then log the swap as a change and update the record.

Secure storage means sensitive documents (passwords, network layouts) are access-controlled and encrypted, yet still available during an outage, for example a protected copy kept off the server, plus an offline or printed copy in a locked location.

Common mistake: documenting once and never updating. Stale diagrams send responders to the wrong device, and expired warranties nobody noticed turn a free repair into a long, costly outage.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is retiring a file server, asset tag AF-0417. It is company-owned (not leased), and the vendor announced end of life (EOL) last year, meaning no more security fixes. The team works through the retirement like this. Step 1: A replacement server was chosen and bought, then installed, patched and monitored, and all client files were copied to it and checked. Step 2: The change is logged in the change-management record, an approved log of every change. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: The old server goes to an electronics recycler, and record AF-0417 is removed from the inventory. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Peel off the asset tag so the number AF-0417 can be reused on the next server bought
Securely wipe the old server's drives or physically destroy them before the hardware leaves the firm
Send the server to the recycler with its drives in place, since recycling the hardware also erases the data
Leave the old server in the inventory as active in case the vendor later releases one more fix
questions.why: The disposal stage requires drives to be securely wiped or physically destroyed so client data cannot leave with the hardware, and only then is the asset removed from inventory.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's inventory shows that the vendor of its warehouse database server has declared the model end of life (EOL). What does that status mean for the server?
choices: The server's lease has ended and it must be returned to the leasing company on a set date
The server's drives have failed and it must be physically destroyed right away
The server has just been bought and is waiting to be installed and patched
The vendor no longer sells or supports the model, so no more fixes will be released for it
questions.why: EOL is the lifecycle stage where the vendor stops selling or supporting a product, so no further fixes arrive. A lease ending, a drive failure and a new purchase are different things.

questions.prompt: A hospital's IT team keeps its admin passwords and network layout diagram in a document stored only on the main file server. An auditor asks them to store it securely. Which approach best meets the goal of secure storage?
choices: Keep the single copy on the file server but rename it so attackers will not recognise it
Keep an access-controlled, encrypted copy off the server, plus a printed copy in a locked cabinet
Print one copy and pin it on the server room wall where responders can see it quickly
Email an unencrypted copy to every IT staff member so that everyone always has one
questions.why: Secure storage means sensitive documents are access-controlled and encrypted yet still available during an outage. A protected copy kept off the server plus a locked offline copy does both.

questions.prompt: At a university data centre, a network switch was moved to a different rack six months ago, but the infrastructure diagram was never changed. During an outage, an engineer follows the diagram and unplugs the wrong device, making the outage longer. Which practice would most directly have prevented this?
choices: Logging the move as a change and updating the diagram whenever equipment is moved
Adding a service level agreement (SLA) that promises higher uptime for the data centre
Replacing the switch as soon as its vendor announced end of life
Recording the switch's serial number when it was first bought
questions.why: The failure came from documenting once and never updating it. Recording each change and updating the diagram keeps responders pointed at the right device.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we bother tracking servers from purchase to disposal and how we store their documentation, including one tradeoff in how we store it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every server gets an asset tag recorded with its model, serial number, location, purchase proof, whether it is owned or leased, and warranty dates. We follow it through procurement, usage, end of life, and disposal, where we wipe or destroy the drives and retire the record. That way when hardware fails we instantly know who supports it and whether repair is covered, and nothing with company data leaves the building unwiped. Alongside that we keep diagrams, baselines, configurations, recovery steps, and a change log, updated after every change. The tradeoff is in storage: sensitive docs must be locked down and encrypted, but if they are too locked down or only live on the server they describe, nobody can reach them during an outage. So we keep a protected copy elsewhere and an offline copy in a secure location.
rubricPoints: Assets are tracked with a tag and a record of model, serial, location, ownership and warranty.
The lifecycle runs procurement, usage, end of life, then secure disposal or recycling.
Documentation includes diagrams, baselines, configurations, recovery steps and change records, kept current.
Sensitive documents need access control and encryption.
Tradeoff: security must not block availability during an outage, so copies live off the server and offline.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly terms, record contents and lifecycle stages to recognise, and no current mission or planned engine exercises inventory or documentation handling directly.

lessons.plain: Data security is about protecting the information itself, not just the server it lives on. Three ideas work together. Encryption scrambles data so only someone holding the right secret key can read it. A retention policy is a rule that says how long each kind of data must be kept and when it must be deleted. Lifecycle management means planning what happens to data from the moment it is created until it is destroyed. Think of a doctor's office: patient files go in a locked cabinet (encryption), are kept for a set number of years (retention), and are then shredded on schedule (end of lifecycle).
lessons.guessPrompt: If someone steals a hard drive from a server, what would have to be true about the data on it for the theft to do no real harm?
lessons.teach:
Data security means protecting information wherever it sits or travels. Three tools cover this objective.

Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable data (ciphertext) using a key, which is a secret value. Only someone with the right key can reverse it. Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as a whole disk, a volume or a database file, so a stolen drive is useless. Encryption in transit protects data moving across a network, for example with TLS (Transport Layer Security), the protocol behind HTTPS, so an eavesdropper sees only noise.

A retention policy is a written rule stating how long each type of data must be kept and when it must be deleted. Laws, contracts and business needs drive it. A legal hold is an order that pauses deletion for data tied to a lawsuit or investigation. Lifecycle management means handling data through every stage: create, store, use, share, archive (move to cheaper, slower storage) and destroy, with rules at each step.

Why it works: encryption shrinks the job of protecting lots of data down to protecting one small key. Retention limits how much data exists to be stolen, leaked or demanded.
