The server has four 2 TB drives. The database makes many small writes all day. It must keep running if one drive fails and must stay reasonably fast while that happens. It will need about 3 TB within two years. RAID (redundant array of independent disks) combines several drives so they act as one, for speed, protection, or both. Your manager suggests RAID 5, which spreads data plus parity across all drives and survives one drive failure. Parity is calculated recovery information that lets the array rebuild a lost drive's data. Your manager says RAID 5 gives the most space. RAID 10 is the other option: drives are paired as mirrors, where each drive in a pair holds an identical copy, and data is then striped across the pairs. Striping means splitting data into chunks spread over several drives.

The server also has a BMC (baseboard management controller). This is a small separate computer on the motherboard that works even when the main operating system is frozen, as long as the server has power. Vendors give it brand names such as Dell iDRAC or HPE iLO. Its dedicated management port is cabled to a separate management network. Reaching a server through a tool like this, instead of through its normal operating system and network, is called out-of-band management. The drive bays are hot-swappable, meaning a drive can be pulled and replaced while the server stays powered on and running.

Six months after installation, at 2 a.m., monitoring shows the database server has stopped responding on the normal network. The data center is three hours' drive away. Once you get in, you also find that drive 2 shows an amber fault light.

1. Say where in the rack you would mount the server, and how you would connect its power and handle airflow, including the U20 gap. Give a reason for each choice.
2. Choose RAID 5 or RAID 10 for this database. Show the usable capacity of each with four 2 TB drives, and explain your choice to your manager.
3. Explain how you would find out what is wrong with the frozen server and try to recover it without driving to the site.
4. Describe how you would replace the failed drive 2 safely, and what you would watch for afterwards.
subParts: RAID level choice and usable capacity
modelAnswer: Mount the server low in the rack, at U3-U4, just above the UPS. Heavy equipment goes near the bottom so the rack's center of gravity stays low and it is less likely to tip, especially when the server is slid out on its rails. Lifting 38 kg up to U38 is also risky, so use two people or a lift and install the rails first. Plug power supply 1 into PDU A (circuit 1) and power supply 2 into PDU B (circuit 2). If either PDU or either building circuit fails, the other supply keeps the server running. Plugging both supplies into the same PDU would waste the redundancy, because one failure would take down both. Mount the server with its front facing the cold aisle and its back facing the hot aisle, matching its front-to-back fan direction. Mounted backwards, it would pull in other equipment's hot exhaust and overheat. Fit a blanking panel over the empty U20 gap so hot air from the back cannot loop through the hole to the front and be pulled back in. Route and label cables so they do not block the rear exhaust.

Choose RAID 10. Usable capacity: RAID 10 mirrors every drive, so half the raw space is usable: 4 x 2 TB = 8 TB raw, divided by 2 = 4 TB usable. RAID 5 loses one drive's worth of space to parity: (4 - 1) x 2 TB = 6 TB usable. Both survive one drive failure, and 4 TB still covers the 3 TB needed in two years. RAID 10 fits this workload better for two reasons. First, every small write on RAID 5 means reading the old data and parity, recalculating parity, and writing both back. This extra work, called the write penalty, slows a write-heavy database. RAID 10 just writes the data to both drives in a mirror pair. Second, when a drive fails, RAID 5 has to rebuild the missing data from parity on every remaining drive. That is slow, puts heavy load on all of them, and leaves no protection if a second drive fails during the rebuild. RAID 10 rebuilds by copying from the one surviving mirror partner, so performance holds up better. The mistake to avoid is choosing a RAID level by capacity alone. The extra 2 TB from RAID 5 is not needed here, and it comes at the cost of slower writes and a riskier rebuild.

Connect to the server's BMC (for example iDRAC or iLO) over the separate management network. The BMC has its own network port and runs independently of the operating system, so it still answers when the OS is frozen. Through the BMC: check the hardware health and event logs, which would show the drive 2 fault, plus any power, temperature, or memory errors. Open the remote console to see the actual screen, such as a hang or an error message. If the OS is truly hung, use the BMC's remote power control to do a graceful reset or power cycle, then watch the boot through the console. This avoids a six-hour round trip. Do not guess and wait until morning, and do not assume a remote desktop or SSH session will work, because those depend on the OS that has frozen. After recovery, note the cause found in the logs.

First confirm which drive has failed, using the BMC or RAID controller logs together with the amber fault light, so you pull the correct drive. Pulling a healthy drive by mistake could take the array down. Check that the array is degraded but still online (RAID 10 survives one failure). Get a replacement of the same type and at least the same capacity. Because the bays are hot-swappable, release and pull the failed drive and insert the new one while the server stays powered on and the database keeps running. No shutdown or outage is needed. The RAID controller should then start rebuilding, copying data from the surviving mirror partner onto the new drive. Watch the rebuild progress in the controller or BMC until the array reports healthy again. During the rebuild the array has no spare protection for that pair, so avoid extra load and maintenance work if you can, and confirm your backups are current. Afterwards, check the logs for errors on the other drives.

scenarios.title: Bringing the Order-Tracking Server into Production at Harbor Lane Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Harbor Lane Logistics, a fictional shipping company, as a junior server administrator. The team is replacing an old machine that runs the company's order-tracking application, the program warehouse staff use to look up where each parcel is. Your lead hands you a new physical server and asks you to prepare it properly, not just click through a default install.

Here is what you know. The server has one 4 TB disk that will hold the operating system and the application data. Its firmware, the built-in startup software that runs before the operating system, is UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface), the modern replacement for the older BIOS (Basic Input/Output System). Before installing, you must choose a partition table, which is the map at the start of a disk that records where each partition (a separate section of the disk) begins and ends. The two common types are MBR (Master Boot Record), the older style, and GPT (GUID Partition Table), the newer style. You must also choose a file system, the method the operating system uses to organise files inside a partition, such as NTFS (New Technology File System) on Windows or ext4 (fourth extended file system) on Linux.

On the network, most office laptops get their addresses from DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), a service that hands out IP addresses automatically and can give a device a different address later. Staff reach the application by typing the name orders.harborlane.local, which DNS (Domain Name System), the service that translates names into IP addresses, must point at this server. The building's switches are divided into VLANs (virtual local area networks), which are logical groups of ports that keep traffic separate even though they share the same physical switch. There is a VLAN for staff laptops and a separate VLAN for servers.

Finally, managers say that if order tracking stops during a shift, trucks cannot be loaded, so they want a second identical server added. The application can only run on one server at a time because it writes to a single shared database. Your lead mentions two high-availability options. A failover cluster is a group of servers that watch each other; in an active-passive cluster one node (a member server) does the work while the other waits, and they exchange a heartbeat, a regular small check-in message, so the standby can take over if the active node goes silent. A load balancer is a device or service that spreads incoming requests across several servers that all work at the same time.

1. Choose the partition table type for the 4 TB disk and a suitable file system, and explain why the other partition table type would be a problem.
2. Decide how the server should get its IP address and how staff will reach it by name, and say which VLAN it belongs on.
3. Choose between an active-passive failover cluster and a load balancer for this application, and explain how failover would happen.
4. Name one common mistake when setting up the cluster heartbeat or failover, and describe what would happen to the running system as a result.
modelAnswer: Use GPT. The server boots with UEFI, which is designed to start from GPT disks, and GPT can address disks far larger than 2 TB and allows many partitions. MBR can only use about 2 TB of a disk, so on this 4 TB disk roughly half the space would be unusable, and it limits the number of primary partitions to four. For the file system, choose one suited to a server workload with large files and permissions, such as NTFS if the operating system is Windows or ext4 (or a similar modern Linux file system) if it is Linux. A common mistake is accepting an MBR default; the consequence is a server that appears to have only about 2 TB of storage and runs out of space early.

Give the server a static IP address, meaning one set by hand that never changes (or, at minimum, a DHCP reservation that always hands it the same address). A server that other systems depend on must not have its address change, because anything pointing at the old address would break. Then create a DNS A record (a record that maps a name to an IPv4 address) so orders.harborlane.local resolves to that static address; staff type the name and DNS returns the IP. Place the server on the server VLAN, not the staff laptop VLAN, so server traffic is kept separate from user devices and access between them can be controlled. Mistake to avoid: leaving it on ordinary DHCP, which can later give it a new address so the DNS record points at the wrong machine and the application becomes unreachable.

Choose an active-passive failover cluster. A load balancer only helps when several servers can do the work at the same time, but this application can only run on one server at once because it writes to a single shared database. In the cluster, server A is active and serves staff, while server B is passive. The two nodes send heartbeat messages at regular intervals. Traced step by step: server A fails, its heartbeats stop, server B notices the missed heartbeats, server B starts the application and takes over the shared database and the cluster's shared IP address or name, and staff reconnect to the same name without needing to know which physical server is now running it. Users may see a short interruption during the switch, but service resumes without anyone rebuilding a server.

One common mistake is sending the heartbeat over a single network path, the same busy link that carries user traffic, with no backup path. If that link becomes congested or fails while both servers are actually still healthy, each node stops hearing the other and assumes the other has died. Both may then try to become active and write to the shared database at once, a situation called split-brain, which can corrupt the order data. Another acceptable answer: never testing failover, so the first real failure reveals that server B cannot start the application, and order tracking stays down during a shift. The fix is a dedicated or redundant heartbeat path, a tie-breaking mechanism such as a quorum (a voting rule that decides which side may stay active), and scheduled failover tests.

scenarios.title: Retiring and Replacing the Billing Server at Harborline Freight
scenarios.scenario:
Harborline Freight is a fictional shipping company. Its old billing server, BILL-01, is being retired. Retiring a server and removing it from service for good is called decommissioning. BILL-01 holds customer names, addresses, and stored payment details. It has two kinds of storage. The first is four spinning hard disk drives (HDDs), which store data magnetically on metal platters. The second is two solid-state drives (SSDs), which store data on flash memory chips with no moving parts. The company's retention policy is a written rule saying how long each type of data must be kept and when it must be destroyed. It says billing records older than seven years must be destroyed, and the records on BILL-01 have already been copied to the new server.

A new server, BILL-02, will take over. During the last security review, an auditor found three problems on the old server. First, anyone who stole a drive could read the files directly, because nothing was encrypted. Encryption means scrambling data so it can only be read with the right key. Second, administrators logged in with only a password. Third, the server ran services nobody used, such as an old file-transfer service and a print spooler. A service is a background program that waits for network requests or does work on its own.

You are the junior server administrator. Your manager asks you the following.

1. Choose a destruction method for BILL-01's four HDDs and two SSDs that makes the customer data unrecoverable. Explain why one popular method works on one drive type but not the other.

2. Describe the paperwork and tracking steps needed so Harborline can prove the drives were destroyed and the server left its records properly.

3. Name the control that fixes the auditor's first finding on BILL-02, and explain what it protects against.

4. Name the specific controls that fix the auditor's second and third findings on BILL-02, and explain why each one reduces risk.
subParts: Asset tracking and proof of destruction
Encryption at rest on the new server
MFA and hardening for the new server
modelAnswer: Because the drives hold sensitive customer and payment data, use physical destruction that the data cannot survive. Shredding is the strongest choice for both drive types. A shredder is a machine that grinds a drive into small pieces. For the HDDs, degaussing is also valid. A degausser applies a very strong magnetic field that scrambles the magnetic patterns on the platters. This usually ruins the drive as well. Degaussing does NOT work on the SSDs, because SSDs store data electrically in flash chips, not magnetically, so the magnetic field leaves the data readable. The SSDs must be shredded, or crushed or disintegrated so the memory chips themselves are physically broken. A common mistake is running a simple delete or quick format and calling it done. That only removes the pointers to the files, and recovery tools can often get the data back. The result could be a data breach after the hardware leaves the building.

Record each drive in the asset inventory before removal. An asset inventory is the company's list of hardware, with serial numbers, locations, and status. Keep a chain of custody, meaning a written log of who handled the drives, when, and where they went. That way none can go missing between the rack and the destruction point. If an outside company does the destruction, get a certificate of destruction. This is a signed document listing the serial numbers destroyed, the method used, and the date. Then update the inventory to mark BILL-01 and its drives as retired or destroyed. Send the remaining non-storage parts, such as the chassis, power supplies, and fans, to an approved electronics recycler instead of the trash. A common mistake is skipping the serial-number match. If an auditor later asks about one specific drive, the company cannot prove what happened to it.

Turn on encryption at rest on BILL-02. Encryption at rest means the data is stored on the disks in scrambled form and is only unscrambled when an authorized system with the correct key reads it. This can be full-disk encryption, which covers the whole drive, or encryption of the specific volumes holding billing data. It protects against someone who physically steals or removes a drive and plugs it into another computer. Without the key, they see only unreadable data. The encryption keys must be stored and backed up separately from the drives. If the key is lost, the company loses its own data too. If the key is taped to the server, the protection is meaningless.

For the password-only logins, require multifactor authentication (MFA) for all administrator accounts. MFA means proving identity with two or more different types of factor: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone app code or hardware token), or something you are (a fingerprint). MFA reduces risk because a stolen or guessed password alone is no longer enough to log in. For the unused services, harden the server. Hardening means reducing ways in by removing what is not needed and keeping what remains up to date. Disable or uninstall the unused file-transfer service and print spooler. Every running service is a possible entry point, and an unused one is rarely watched or patched, so attackers can exploit its flaws. Hardening should also include applying current OS updates before BILL-02 goes live. A common mistake is only stopping a service without setting it to disabled, so it starts again after the next reboot.

scenarios.title: Monday Morning at Brightwater Logistics: One Server, Three Symptoms
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Logistics, a fictional regional shipping company, runs its order-tracking application on a single physical server called BWL-APP01. You are the junior server technician on duty. Before you start, here are the terms you will need.

A fault domain is the broad area where a problem lives: hardware (the physical parts), software (the operating system and applications), or network (the cables, switches and settings that move data between machines). Good troubleshooting means finding the fault domain from evidence before you change anything, because a fix aimed at the wrong domain wastes time and can create new problems.

RAID (redundant array of independent disks) combines several drives so the server keeps working if one fails. In RAID 5, data plus recovery information called parity is spread across at least three drives, so any one drive can fail without data loss. A RAID 5 array with one failed drive is called degraded: it still works, but it is slower and has no protection left, so a second failure destroys the array. Rebuilding is the process where the RAID controller (the card that manages the array) recreates the missing data onto a replacement drive.

The event log is the operating system's record of errors, warnings and service starts and stops. A patch is an update to software, and a rollback means removing a patch to return to the previous working state.

Duplex describes how a network link talks. Full duplex sends and receives at the same time. Half duplex takes turns. If one end of a cable is set to full and the other to half, this is a duplex mismatch: the link stays up and ping replies still come back, but heavy traffic collides, gets resent, and becomes very slow.

In disaster recovery (DR), the plan for getting services back after a serious failure, two targets matter. RPO (recovery point objective) is the most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is the longest the service can be down. A backup job that reports success only proves files were copied; only a restore test, which means actually restoring the backup to a separate machine and checking that the application works, proves the backup is usable.

Here is what you find. On Sunday night an automatic OS patch was installed and BWL-APP01 rebooted. On Monday the order-tracking web page shows an error. The event log shows the order-tracking service failed to start right after the reboot, with an error naming a file changed by Sunday's patch. Ping to the server works, other services on the server run normally, and the power supplies show green lights.

The RAID management tool reports the RAID 5 array as degraded: drive bay 2 shows failed and its amber light is on. Drives in bays 1, 3 and 4 show healthy. There is no hot spare (an idle drive the controller uses automatically when one fails).

Staff at the warehouse say that even before the patch, copying large shipping reports to BWL-APP01 has been painfully slow, though small requests work. You check the server's network card: 1 Gbps, full duplex, set manually. The switch port it plugs into is set to automatically negotiate and currently shows 1 Gbps, half duplex.

Finally, your manager says the nightly backup has shown success every night for a year, the business has set an RPO of 24 hours and an RTO of 4 hours, and nobody has ever restored from it.

1. Identify the fault domain of the order-tracking outage, state the evidence that points there, and describe the safe corrective step.
2. Explain what the degraded RAID 5 state means for the risk to the server, and give the correct order of actions to resolve it, including one mistake to avoid.
3. Diagnose the slow large file transfers, explain why small requests and ping still work, and state the fix.
4. Explain why the year of successful backup reports does not prove Brightwater can recover, and describe how you would validate the DR plan against its RPO and RTO.
modelAnswer: The fault domain is software, specifically the Sunday OS patch. The evidence: the event log shows the order-tracking service failed to start immediately after the patch reboot, with an error naming a file the patch changed. Hardware and network are ruled out for this symptom because power supply lights are green, other services run normally, and ping works. The safe step is to roll back the patch (or apply a vendor fix for that file), restart the service, confirm in the event log that it now starts cleanly, test the web page, and record the change. Replacing hardware or changing network settings would be aimed at the wrong domain.

Degraded means the RAID 5 array is still serving data using the three healthy drives and parity, but it is slower and has no redundancy left; if a second drive fails before a rebuild finishes, the whole array and its data are lost. Correct order: first confirm a current, usable backup exists, because the array is unprotected. Then identify the failed drive using the RAID tool and the amber light in bay 2, replace that exact drive with a compatible one, and let the controller rebuild. Monitor the rebuild until the array reports healthy, and consider adding a hot spare. The mistake to avoid is pulling the wrong drive, such as a healthy one in bay 1, 3 or 4; removing a second drive from a degraded RAID 5 array destroys it.

This is a duplex mismatch, a network fault. The server card is manually set to 1 Gbps full duplex, while the auto-negotiating switch port has fallen back to half duplex. Small requests and ping still work because the link is up and light traffic rarely triggers collisions. Large transfers send heavy traffic in both directions at once, so the half duplex side sees collisions, data is resent, and throughput collapses. The fix is to make both ends match: set both to auto-negotiate, or set both manually to 1 Gbps full duplex. Then confirm both show full duplex and retest a large file copy.

A success message only shows that the job copied data; it does not prove the data is complete, uncorrupted, or able to bring the application back, and it says nothing about how long recovery takes. To validate, perform a restore test: restore the latest backup to a separate test machine, start the order-tracking application, and check that it works and its data is correct. Check the newest restored data is no older than 24 hours, meeting the RPO. Time the whole restore from start until the application is usable and confirm it is under 4 hours, meeting the RTO. Record the results, fix any gaps, and repeat the test on a regular schedule.
